Quantum complexity across thermal phase transition in the transverse field Ising chain with long-range couplings

M. Adhikary1⋆\star, N. Ranabhat1,2 and M. Collura1,3†\dagger

1 International School for Advanced Studies (SISSA), via Bonomea 265, 34136 Trieste, Italy

2 University of Maryland, Baltimore County, Baltimore, Maryland, USA

3 INFN Sezione di Trieste, 34136 Trieste, Italy

⋆\star madhikar@sissa.it , †\dagger mcollura@sissa.it

Abstract

We investigate the behavior of the Schmidt gap, the von Neumann entanglement entropy, and the non-stabiliserness in proximity to the classical phase transition of the one-dimensional long-range transverse-field Ising model (LRTFIM). Leveraging the time-dependent variational principle (TDVP) within a tensor-network formulation, we simulate thermal states through their purified tensor-network representations. Our results show that these observables—typically regarded as hallmarks of quantum criticality—exhibit pronounced and coherent signatures even at a classical thermal transition, highlighting the emergence of quantum complexity as the system nears thermal criticality.

1 Introduction

Understanding the interplay between classical statistical phenomena and quantum complexity is a fundamental challenge in many-body physics. In particular, classical thermal phase transitions, while traditionally described through macroscopic order parameters and equilibrium statistical mechanics [34, 42], can reveal subtle quantum signatures when examined through the lens of purified quantum states. This perspective is particularly relevant for systems where high control over individual constituents is possible, such as trapped-ion quantum simulators.

A paradigmatic platform for exploring such phenomena is the long-range one-dimensional transverse-field Ising model (LRTFIM) at finite temperature T [53, 19]. In this model, spins interact via a power-law exchange coupling that decays with distance as d−�d^{-\alpha}, and are subject to a transverse magnetic field hh. The LRTFIM exhibits a rich phase diagram in the temperature–field plane, with a quantum phase transition at T=0T=0 from a paramagnetic to a ferromagnetic phase [53]. The critical behavior of the model depends sensitively on the interaction exponent �\alpha, which controls the decay of the exchange interactions, interpolating between a mean-field-like regime for small �\alpha and short-range interactions for large �\alpha [19, 23]. Beyond equilibrium, the model has attracted attention for its non-equilibrium dynamics, including interesting correlation propagation and entanglement growth [26, 50, 6, 51], making it a versatile platform for quantum simulation, quantum information, and quantum computation studies [9].

To probe quantum aspects of thermal transitions in the LRTFIM, we employ tensor network methods, representing the thermal state in a purified form via the Matrix Product Density Operator (MPDO) ansatz [59, 18]. Purification allows any mixed state to be encoded as a pure state in an enlarged Hilbert space, introducing ancillary degrees of freedom that encode classical statistical mixing. In this framework, we can efficiently compute the entanglement of the purified state, the Schmidt gap of the entanglement spectrum, and measures of quantum complexity such as non-stabilizerness (“magic”). Importantly, these quantities capture genuine quantum correlations that are not apparent in the classical density matrix, highlighting how classical thermal states can encode nontrivial quantum features at criticality [1, 39, 55].

Non-stabilizerness, quantified via stabilizer Rényi entropies and related measures, provides a rigorous lens for characterizing the computational resources inherent in quantum states [58, 37]. While entanglement alone is insufficient to guarantee quantum computational advantage, stabilizer states being highly entangled yet classically simulable, non-stabilizerness captures the “magic” resources required for universal quantum computation [58, 7, 10, 8]. In our analysis, we evaluate these measures for finite-size systems and demonstrate that pronounced peaks in non-stabilizerness emerge at the thermal phase transition, signaling a sharp increase in quantum complexity precisely at criticality.

Methodologically, we obtain the purified states as Matrix Product States (MPS) using the Time-Dependent Variational Principle (TDVP) [45, 32]. We focus on two representative values of the transverse field, h=0.0h=0.0 and 0.30.3, and two interaction exponents, �=0.8\alpha=0.8 and 1.81.8, while scanning the temperature to cross the paramagnetic-to-ferromagnetic transition. This procedure yields the MPS representation of the purified state at each temperature, enabling a direct evaluation of entanglement and magic.

In this work, we combine the LRTFIM at finite temperature, tensor network purification, and measures of entanglement and non-stabilizerness to provide a unified picture of how classical phase transitions can manifest quantum complexity. Our results demonstrate that even classically describable mixed states exhibit rich quantum structure in their purified representation, bridging classical statistical mechanics, quantum information theory, and experimental quantum simulation platforms.

2 Model

The LRTFIM serves as a paradigmatic model for studying phase transitions and critical phenomena. It exhibits not only the ground state and finite-temperature phase transition but also the dynamical phase transition due to the emergent confinement phenomenon. The model Hamiltonian is given by,

H^=−1K�​(N)∑i>j|J||i−j|�sziszj−h∑isxi\displaystyle\begin{split}\hat{H}&=-\frac{1}{K_{\alpha}(N)}\sum_{i>j}\frac{|J|}{|i-j|^{\alpha}}s^{z}_{i}s^{z}_{j}-h\sum_{i}s^{x}_{i}\end{split} (1)

Here, si�s^{\nu}_{i} represents the spin one-half operator in �=x,y,z\nu=x,y,z direction at site ii. The spins interact via a power-law potential that decays as the inverse of their separation distance raised to the power �\alpha. The parameter interaction strength |J||J| is set to unity and rescaled via the Kać normalization factor K�(N)=1/(N−1)∑i=1N(N−i)/i�K_{\alpha}(N)=1/(N-1)\sum_{i=1}^{N}(N-i)/i^{\alpha}, to keep the energy per spin finite in thermodynamic limit for �<1\alpha<1 scenario and just to put a energy rescaling for �>1\alpha>1 case. The transverse magnetic field hh sets the strength of the off-diagonal term of the Hamiltonian responsible for the non-trivial dynamics. The parameter �\alpha tunes the range of spin-spin interaction in the model. At two extremes, the model becomes integrable and can be solved by exact analytical and numerical methods [12, 44]. At �=∞\alpha=\infty, the model becomes the nearest-neighbor transverse field Ising model (TFIM), which can be effectively solved by mapping onto spinless fermions through the Jordan-Wigner transformation. This short-range universality class persists for �≥3\alpha\geq 3. In the opposite limit, �=0\alpha=0, the Hamiltonian can be written in terms of a collective sum of single operators, S�=∑is�S^{\nu}=\sum_{i}s^{\nu}, and its thermodynamic limit properties are exactly captured by the mean field theory. More generally, the system belongs to the mean-field universality class for �≤1.5\alpha\leq 1.5  [19].

For strictly local interactions, one-dimensional models do not exhibit any finite-temperature phase transitions [47], as any ferromagnetic order is destroyed at T>0T>0. By contrast, long-range interactions increase the effective connectivity between spins, effectively raising their spatial dimension [28, 48, 14, 16]. Quantitatively, a dd-dimensional system with couplings decaying as J⁡(r)∝r−�J(r)\propto r^{-\alpha} displays universal behavior equivalent to a locally interacting system in an effective dimension deff=2​(d+z)/(�−d)d_{\text{eff}}=2(d+z)/(\alpha-d), where zz is the dynamical critical exponent [12, 15, 41]. Within the effective-dimension picture, lowering �\alpha raises deffd_{\mathrm{eff}} across the thresholds separating short-range–like, nontrivial long-range, and mean-field regimes, providing a unified rationale for both the emergence of thermal order and the continuous evolution of critical exponents in the long-range transverse-field Ising model [23]. The long-range power-law couplings render domain walls increasingly costly with their linear extent: the excess energy of a domain of length ℓ\ell scales as EDW​(ℓ)∼ℓ 2−�E_{\mathrm{DW}}(\ell)\sim\ell^{\,2-\alpha}. For 1<�<21<\alpha<2, this scaling overcomes the configurational entropy that drives kink proliferation in models with local interaction, thereby stabilizing long-range ferromagnetic order at finite temperature [44, 45, 46, 54, 40]. In one dimension, the mechanism yields a thermal transition for 1<�≤21<\alpha\leq 2 with a low temperature ferromagnetic phase transitioning to a high temperature paramagnetic phase, whereas for �>2\alpha>2 the model reverts to short-range behavior with no finite-TT transition [31, 15].

3 Quantum-inspired probes for classical thermal transition

Traditionally, thermal phase transitions are identified by the expectation values of local order parameters and their susceptibilities, which change from nonzero to zero across a symmetry-breaking transition. For the LRTFIM, prior work has characterized the transition using such order-parameter diagnostics [23]. Here, we adopt a complementary, order-parameter-agnostic, quantum-information-inspired approach. Specifically, we construct the thermal Gibbs state in the locally purified tensor network representation as introduced by Werner et al. [61], ��=X�​X�†\rho_{\beta}=X_{\beta}X_{\beta}^{\dagger}. where the physical indices sis_{i} and the Kraus indices kik_{i} lie in range 1≤si≤d1\leq s_{i}\leq d, 1≤�i≤K1\leq\kappa_{i}\leq K, respectively. In this article, we will calculate two non-classical parameters directly over the purification |X�⟩|X_{\beta}\rangle to study the thermal phase transition,

3.1 Schmidt gap of entanglement spectrum

In the field of quantum many-body physics, Schmidt eigenvalues provide a crucial measure to characterize the entanglement spectrum. Given a pure state |X�⟩\ket{X_\beta}, these eigenvalues can be obtained for a given bipartition ( say AA and BB ) of the system through Schmidt decomposition, |X�⟩=∑i�i​|iA⟩⊗|iB⟩\ket{X_\beta}=\sum_{i}\lambda_{i}\ket{i_A}\otimes\ket{i_B}, where {�i}\{\lambda_{i}\}’s are the Schmidt coefficients and the ∑i\sum_{i} runs over the nonzero terms. The gap between the first two largest coefficients, known as the Schmidt gap (SG), is considered an important order parameter to identify quantum phase transition [11, 22, 38, 56, 43, 24, 52].

The ground state study of TFIM reveals a transition of SG from 00 to 11 as hh changes from 00 to a higher value [56]. SG taking the value 11 is equivalent to one of the Schmidt vectors being dominant, and for TFIM, this implies that the system belongs to a product state. Whereas a 00 value of S​GSG for a lower value of hh implies the presence of the GHZ-like state ( Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger ), i.e., a mixture of |11⋯1>|11\cdots 1> and |00⋯0>|00\cdots 0>. Such interesting features of SG motivate us to investigate its behavior near the classical phase transition of LRTFIM.

In the present work, we consider the central partition of a pure state MPS |X�⟩\ket{X_\beta} for the open spin chain of length NN. The central partition is a reliable measure of the maximum entanglement attained by the system. Thereafter, we calculate �\Delta, defined as the difference between the squares of the two largest Schmidt eigenvalues of the entanglement spectrum, together with its susceptibility as a function of �\beta,

�=�12−�22�=∂�/∂�\displaystyle\begin{split}\Delta&=\lambda_{1}^{2}-\lambda_{2}^{2}\\ \chi&=\partial\Delta/\partial\beta\end{split} (4)

Another interesting quantity related to the Schmidt coefficients is the Von Neumann entanglement entropy (S) of the complete system, defined as,

S=−∑i�i2log2�i2S=-\sum_{i}\lambda_{i}^{2}\log_{2}\lambda_{i}^{2} (5)

This is a well-studied measure of quantum correlation for a pure state. At zero temperature, as hh goes from 00 to 11, S/NS/N goes from 1/N1/N to 00 showing a singularity at the criticality, [35, 13]. The nature of this divergence depends upon �\alpha. To analyze the quantum complexity of the model near the classical critical point, we calculate �,�,S\Delta,~\chi,~S for system sizes N=16,32,64,100,250,300,350,400N=16,32,64,100,250,300,350,400. We discuss the results in Sec . 4.

3.2 Stabilizer Rényi Entropy (SRE)

Nonstabilizerness or quantum magic, MM is considered to be a good measure of constructional complexity of a quantum state from a quantum technological perspective [37, 36]. It gives us a deep insight into how hard it is to prepare the corresponding state in a classical computer. For a stabilizer state, MM is always zero, thus MM behaves in a different way than the standard entanglement. A non-zero MM mirrors the quantum complexity in the state. Motivated by such an interesting character of MM, in the second part of our analysis, we focus on estimating the quantum magic MM by means of calculating the n-SRE of the pure state MPS found as a result of TDVP. We follow the perfect sampling of the Pauli string framework to calculate MnM_{n}, as prescribed in  [33, 25]. For a N−N-qubit system in a pure state �=| ⟩​⟨ |\rho=\ket{\psi}\bra{\psi}, the n−n- SRE is defined as following [37],

Mn​(�)=11−n​log​∑�∈𝒫N12N​T​r​[�​�]2​nM_{n}(\rho)=\frac{1}{1-n}\log\sum_{\sigma\in\mathcal{P}_{N}}\frac{1}{2^{N}}Tr[\rho\boldsymbol{\sigma}]^{2n} (6)

Here, �\boldsymbol{\sigma} denotes a string of NN Pauli operators, �=∏i=1N�i\boldsymbol{\sigma}=\prod_{i=1}^{N}\sigma_{i}. Each �i\sigma_{i} can take four values {�0,�1,�2,�3}\{\sigma^{0},\sigma^{1},\sigma^{2},\sigma^{3}\}. The set 𝒫N\mathcal{P}_{N}contains all possible such strings, and therefore has the size 4N4^{N}. For a certain pure state | ⟩\ket{\psi}, we construct the corresponding pure state density matrix �\rho. If we regard the positive real valued function, ∏�(�)=(1/2N)​T​r​[�​�]2\boldsymbol{\prod}_{\rho}(\boldsymbol{\sigma})=(1/2^{N})Tr[\rho\boldsymbol{\sigma}]^{2}, as a probability distribution over �\boldsymbol{\sigma}, Eq. 6 takes the form of a standard Rényi entropy . This interpretation is valid since ∑�∈𝓟𝑵∏�(�)=1\sum_{\boldsymbol{\sigma\in\mathcal{P}_{N}}}\boldsymbol{\prod}_{\rho}(\boldsymbol{\sigma})=1 [37]. With this consideration, n-SRE calculation turns out to be a computation of the average of (n−1)th(n-1)^{\text{th}} power of the distribution function itself. With this simplification, Eq. 6 can be written as Mn​(�)=1/(1−n)​log⁡∏�(�)n−1¯−N​log⁡2M_{n}(\rho)=1/(1-n)\log\overline{\boldsymbol{\prod}_{\rho}(\boldsymbol{\sigma})^{n-1}}-N\log 2, for n>1n>1. 4 Results and Discussion

In Fig. 1, we show the evolution of �\Delta, SS, and �\chi as functions of the inverse temperature �\beta for eight different system sizes NN, while keeping �=1.8\alpha=1.8 in Fig. 1(a) and �=1.8\alpha=1.8 in Fig. 1(b), with h=0.0h=0.0. Focusing on the leftmost panel, which displays �\Delta versus �\beta, we observe that at high temperatures (low �\beta), �≈1\Delta\approx 1. This corresponds to �1≈1\lambda_{1}\approx 1, indicating the absence of quantum entanglement and the classical nature of the thermal state. In this regime, thermal fluctuations dominate and effectively suppress quantum correlations. As �\beta increases, �\Delta decreases smoothly from 11 to 00, with a more rapid decay near the critical point, as evidenced by the �=∂�/∂�\chi=\partial\Delta/\partial\beta plot. At large �\beta, �≈0\Delta\approx 0 signifies the entangled ground state given by an equal superposition of the all-up and all-down spin configurations of the LRTFIM at h=0h=0. The two rightmost panels of Fig. 1 show the entanglement entropy SS as a function of �\beta. Starting from S≈0S\approx 0 at high temperature, SS increases with decreasing temperature, exhibiting a peak before saturating to 11 (note that SS is scaled by log⁡2\log 2). This behavior reflects the transition from a maximally mixed, entanglement-less thermal state at high TT to a GHZ-like entangled state at low TT. The collective temperature dependence of �\Delta, �\chi, and SS thus provides clear signatures of a finite-temperature transition. Fig 1 further illustrates the finite-size effects in these quantities near the transition. We find that the critical inverse temperature �c\beta_{c} is more strongly affected by finite-size effects for �=0.8\alpha=0.8. In this case, the pick in �\chi or SS gradually shifts towards lower �\beta as NN increases. On the other hand, for �=1.8\alpha=1.8, there is no noticeable shift in these picks with increasing NN. The result consistently captures the fact that the finite-size effect is more pronounced in the long-range limit than in the short-range regime. In Sec . 4.1 we analyze the �c\beta_{c}’s through a finite-size scaling of the order parameter �\Delta. Our estimate of �c\beta_{c}’s for both the �\alpha’s are marked through the vertical dashed lines.

In Fig. 2(a) and 2(b), we show the variation of the three quantities �\Delta, SS, and �\chi for two different values of the transverse field h=0.0,0.3h=0.0,0.3, with N=400N=400 and �=1.8\alpha=1.8. As hh increases from 0.00.0 to 0.30.3, the critical features in all three observables shift to larger values of �\beta. Fig. 2(a) shows that the shift is prominent for �=1.8\alpha=1.8. In contrast, for �=0.8\alpha=0.8 we find the shift is less noticeable. Quantitatively, the displacement is approximately �​�∼0.06\Delta\beta\sim 0.06 and ∼0.003\sim 0.003, indicating that the critical temperature decreases more for the short range regime when a nonzero field is applied. See Table 1. This behavior is consistent with the physical expectation that, in the presence of a transverse field, a smaller amount of thermal fluctuation is sufficient to drive the system into the paramagnetic phase [15, 23]. Consequently, the phase transition occurs at a lower temperature for larger magnetic fields, eventually terminating at a quantum critical point located at h=hch=h_{c} at zero temperature. A quick DMRG check yields hc≈1.55​(2)h_{c}\approx 1.55(2) and ≈1.85​(2)\approx 1.85(2) for �=1.8\alpha=1.8 and 0.80.8 respectively. This explains why the observed shift in the critical region between h=0.0h=0.0 and h=0.3h=0.3 remains smaller for the mean-field limit than for the shorter-range limit. Since the numerical cost of the full tensor-network simulations increases substantially with larger hh, we restrict our analysis to these two field values. In Appendix D, we provide the corresponding DMRG results for both values of �\alpha. Similarly, in Fig. 2(c) we compare the evolution of �\Delta, �\chi, and SS as functions of �\beta for �=1.8\alpha=1.8 and �=0.8\alpha=0.8, keeping N=400N=400 and h=0.0h=0.0 fixed. In this case, we observe a noticeable shift of the critical point toward lower values of �\beta as �\alpha decreases. This substantial displacement when moving from �=1.8\alpha=1.8, which lies in the intermediate regime between short- and long-range interactions, to �=0.8\alpha=0.8, which is deep in the mean-field-like regime, is consistent with earlier findings [23]. Next, we perform a finite-size scaling analysis of these three order parameters to estimate the critical inverse temperature �c\beta_{c} for �=0.8,1.8\alpha=0.8,1.8 and h=0.0,0.3h=0.0,0.3.

4.1 Finite size scaling of Schmidt gap

To analyze the finite temperature critical behavior, we perform a finite-size scaling (FSS) analysis following the standard prescription for classical order parameters  [5, 29, 49]. The Schmidt gap �\Delta is a good observable in the study of quantum criticality and is known to exhibit critical finite-size scaling [11, 57]. If it is also a good indicator of thermal phase transition, then near the critical point �c\beta_{c}, �\Delta is expected to obey the universal scaling. According to the recent approach for thermal phase transition, known as Q finite-size scaling (Q-FSS)  [17, 30, 4], this universal scaling can be written as,

�(N,�)=N−�/�~ℱ[(�−�c)N1/�~],\Delta(N,\beta)=N^{-\kappa/\tilde{\nu}}\,\mathcal{F}\!\left[(\beta-\beta_{c})\,N^{1/\tilde{\nu}}\right], (9)

Here ℱ\mathcal{F} is the universal critical scaling function. �~=max​(1,d/du​c)​�\tilde{\nu}=\text{max}(1,d/d_{uc})\nu and �\nu is the correlation length critical exponent. �\kappa is a scaling exponent associated with the Schmidt gap. The quantity dd is the physical dimension of the system, which is 11 in our case, and du​cd_{uc} is the upper critical dimension of the system and is du​c=2​(�−1)d_{uc}=2(\alpha-1) for �∈[1,3]\alpha\in[1,3]. As proposed in the framework of Q-FSS,

�~=�​for​d≤du​c​(�≥1.5)=ddu​c​�​for​d>du​c​(�<1.5)\displaystyle\begin{split}\tilde{\nu}&=\nu~~\text{for}~~d\leq d_{uc}~~(\alpha\geq 1.5)\\ &=\frac{d}{d_{uc}}\nu~~\text{for}~~d>d_{uc}~~(\alpha<1.5)\end{split} (10)

For �≤1.5\alpha\leq 1.5, the model belongs to the mean field critical behavior, and here the renormalization group studies have shown �=1/(�−1)\nu=1/(\alpha-1)  [19]. For the intermediate 1.5<�≤2.01.5<\alpha\leq 2.0, �\nu continuously varies with �\alpha in a nontrivial way  [17, 2], as quantum fluctuation plays an important role here.

The rescaled Schmidt gap �​N�/�~\Delta N^{\kappa/\tilde{\nu}}, when plotted as a function of (�−�c)​N1/�~(\beta-\beta_{c})N^{1/\tilde{\nu}}, should collapse onto a single universal curve for different system sizes NN. In practice, we treat the critical exponents �\kappa and �~\tilde{\nu}, together with the critical inverse temperature �c\beta_{c}, as free fitting parameters to obtain the best data collapse. These exponents provide a quantitative characterization of the critical behavior. We restrict the FSS analysis to system sizes N=200,250,300,350,400N=200,250,300,350,400 and estimate {�c,�,�~}\{\beta_{c},\kappa,\tilde{\nu}\} for the four combination of {�,h}\{\alpha,h\} as summarized in the table below

In Fig. 3(b)(a) and (b), we present the resulting data collapse for �=1.8\alpha=1.8 and �=0.8\alpha=0.8, respectively, at h=0.0h=0.0. We observe that for a fixed field hh, �c\beta_{c} is systematically smaller for �=0.8\alpha=0.8 than for �=1.8\alpha=1.8. Conversely, for fixed �\alpha, increasing the field from h=0.0h=0.0 to h=0.3h=0.3 shifts �c\beta_{c} to larger values. It is also relevant to mention that the same field effects �c\beta_{c} more in the short-range limit than in the long range limit. For zero field �=1.8\alpha=1.8 the system is in the intermediate regime and our data collapse result estimates �~=�=2.41​(3)\tilde{\nu}=\nu=2.41(3). This estimate agrees with the finding of Ricci-Tersenghi et al. [2] where they calculate critical exponents for thermal phase transition for �=1.875,1.654\alpha=1.875,1.654 and find �≈2.425\nu\approx 2.425 and ≈1.976\approx 1.976, respectively by means of Monte Carlo simulation. Our result 2.41​(3)2.41(3) for �=1.8\alpha=1.8 falls between the two �\nu’s that they estimate and lies close to their result for �=1.875\alpha=1.875. We also compare our result with Troung et al. [3] and again find good agreement. Therefore, we can conclude that the Schmidt gap is good enough to capture the thermal critical behavior and is capable of indicating that the system belongs to the Ising universality class. For �=0.8\alpha=0.8, the system lies deep inside the long range regime, and as mentioned before, for this the system should fall under the mean-field universality class. Here, the extraction of �\nu from �~\tilde{\nu} needs a non-trivial rescaling, and it is less well characterized in the literature for �<1\alpha<1  [23]. Our scaling analysis yields �~=2.44​(3)\tilde{\nu}=2.44(3); however, the limited theoretical understanding in this regime restricts a direct quantitative comparison with established results.

4.2 Behavior of the upper bound of magic near criticality

In this part, we analyze the thermal phase transition through the behavior of mnm_{n} as a function of �\beta. As discussed in Sec . 3.2, the fact that each tensor in the MPS representation is a rank-4 effectively doubles the system size for the purposes of computing the nn-SRE, making the calculation equivalent to treating a system of size 2​N2N. This imposes practical limitations on the choice of NN, since larger physical system sizes require substantially more samples 𝒩\mathcal{N} to achieve reliable statistical accuracy, as indicated by Eq. 8. Consequently, in this part of our analysis, we restrict ourselves to comparatively smaller system sizes for evaluating the non-stabilizerness densities mnm_{n}. First we discuss the key features for N=32N=32. In the subsequent subsection we compare the data for N=16,32,64N=16,32,64. For all results presented below, we fix the number of samples to 𝒩=104\mathcal{N}=10^{4}.

Fig. 4(a) shows the evolution of m1m_{1} for h=0.0h=0.0 and h=0.3h=0.3 (blue and orange curves, respectively) at fixed �=1.8\alpha=1.8 and N=32N=32. Similarly, Fig. 4(b) displays the corresponding behavior for �=0.8\alpha=0.8 and �=1.8\alpha=1.8 (blue and orange curves, respectively), with h=0.0h=0.0 and N=32N=32. Figures 4(c) and (d) present the same information for m2m_{2}. At fixed �\alpha, the peak position of m1,2m_{1,2} exhibits only a weak dependence on hh in Fig. 4(a) and (c), whereas the magnitude of m1,2m_{1,2} increases clearly with hh. In contrast, Fig. 4(b) and (d) show a more pronounced shift of peaks toward lower �\beta with nearly identical amplitudes, as �\alpha is reduced from 1.81.8 to 0.80.8, reflecting the distinct universality classes associated with these interaction exponents. These trends are consistent with the behavior of �\Delta, �\chi, and SS discussed earlier. In the zero-field case, for both choices of �\alpha, m1,2m_{1,2} vanishes at small �\beta, then increases as �\beta grows, reaches a maximum, and eventually returns to zero as �→∞\beta\rightarrow\infty. This vanishing of m1,2m_{1,2} in both the �→0\beta\to 0 and �→∞\beta\to\infty limits is expected for the LRTFIM at zero field: the system is maximally mixed at �=0\beta=0 and becomes ferromagnetically ordered at very large �\beta, and both limits correspond to stabilizer states with zero magic. For h=0.3h=0.3, however, m1m_{1} (m2m_{2}) saturates to 0.1341±0.040.1341\pm 0.04 (0.055±0.0120.055\pm 0.012) at large �\beta, as any nonzero field introduces non-stabilizerness into the system. The qualitative features of m1m_{1} and m2m_{2} as functions of �\beta are similar; however, the peak of m2m_{2} is lower and narrower. The statistical error in m1,2m_{1,2} is proportional to m1,2m_{1,2} itself and therefore vanishes when the magic is zero. Near the peak, �​m1∼8%\delta m_{1}\sim 8\% for h=0.0h=0.0, increasing to ∼9%\sim 9\% for h=0.3h=0.3. For m2m_{2}, �​m2\delta m_{2} reaches ∼14%\sim 14\% at zero field and increases to ∼22%\sim 22\% at h=0.3h=0.3 for 𝒩=104\mathcal{N}=10^{4} samples. As discussed in Sec . 3.2, the maximum �​m2\delta m_{2} is significantly larger than the maximum �​m1\delta m_{1}.

As discussed in Sec. 3.2, the quantity mnm_{n} that we compute in this work is not the absolute or “true” magic of the thermal state at inverse temperature �\beta. Rather, it corresponds to a particular choice of purification or embedding of the mixed state into a larger pure-state system. In principle, a more rigorous definition of magic for a mixed state would require a more involved minimization procedure (for example, across different purification schemes) [36, 60]. Because we are not performing this full optimization, our estimate of magic is an upper bound — the actual magic could be strictly lower. Nonetheless, even within our framework, the signal we obtain appears strong enough to reliably detect the thermal phase transition.

4.3 Finite size effect on magic

In Fig.5 we compare the m1m_{1} results for three different system sizes N=16,32,64N=16,32,64 for both �=1.8,0.8\alpha=1.8,0.8. The vertical dashed lines here refer to the �c\beta_{c} that we extract from FSS of the Schmidt gap data for larger NN’s in Sec.4.1. Interestingly, for 1.81.8, the system-size effect is not very prominent. Thus, the signal from the m1m_{1} even for a lower NN is capable of giving a good indication of the critical point. Whereas for 0.80.8 the estimate of �c\beta_{c} from FSS is significantly away from the peaks of the three m1m_{1} curves. Noticeably, the peak shifts towards the dashed line as NN increases from 1616 to 6464. Therefore, the system size effect is larger in �=0.8\alpha=0.8 than in �=1.8\alpha=1.8. This is again consistent with LRTFIM being in the long-range regime for the first value of �\alpha, whereas being in the short range regime for the other. Here we do not show the system size effect for m2m_{2}, as for all sampling purposes we kept 𝒩=104,\mathcal{N}=10^{4}, which is not good enough for N=64N=64 in order to get a lower variance.

5 Conclusion and outlook

In this work, we investigated the classical thermal phase transition of the one-dimensional spin-1/21/2 long-range transverse-field Ising model (LRTFIM), examining two representative regimes: the long-range interacting case with �=0.8\alpha=0.8 and the more short-range-like case with �=1.8\alpha=1.8. Using the TDVP algorithm within the tensor-network framework, we approximated thermal states through their purified MPS representations and analyzed both the Schmidt gap, capturing quantum entanglement, and the stabilizer Rényi entropies (SREs), probing quantum magic and numerical complexity.

For the entanglement study, we considered eight different system sizes and extracted critical temperatures and critical exponents via a finite-size scaling analysis of the Schmidt gap for the five largest systems (N=200,250,300,350,400N=200,250,300,350,400). Our estimate of �\nu seems quite consistent with previous work, at least in the short range limit. For the magic analysis, we restricted ourselves to the three smaller system sizes (N=16,32,64N=16,32,64) due to the computational cost of evaluating SREs. Remarkably, both indicators independently signal the thermal transition: the Schmidt gap collapses from 11 to 00, while the magic displays a pronounced peak as a function of �\beta. For �=1.8\alpha=1.8, the transition points inferred from these two diagnostics agree well; for �=0.8\alpha=0.8, quantitative differences appear, reflecting stronger finite-size effects in the long-range regime. This distinction between mild and strong size dependence provides a consistent picture of the crossover between short-range and long-range behavior.

It is important to emphasize that, for the specific class of purification we employ, our analysis does not yield the true magic or entanglement of the thermal mixed state: both quantities are affected by the MPS purification ansatz and by the finite bond dimension. Nevertheless, the approximation is sufficiently robust for the purpose of locating the thermal transition, which is the primary objective of our study.

Several natural directions emerge from our work. First, one may explore alternative tensor-network-based purification, such as non-locally purified tensor networks, isometric MPO encoding, or hybrid Clifford-assisted constructions. Different purification schemes may reduce the bias associated with the chosen ansatz, potentially yielding more accurate estimates of magic for mixed states and improving numerical stability near criticality.

Second, it would be interesting to investigate whether SREs for mixed states can be computed directly within an MPDO representation, without relying on a fixed purification. Although it remains unclear whether SREs for mixed states constitute a fully faithful measure of magic, they still represent a meaningful indicator, as they quantify the entropy of the state’s probability distribution in the Pauli basis. Developing efficient contraction or sampling strategies for MPDO-based SREs (as preliminarily depicted in the Appendix C) could significantly extend the applicability of magic diagnostics to larger system sizes or to real-time dynamics.

Finally, our results highlight the potential of complexity-based markers, such as magic and features of the entanglement spectrum, as complementary probes of phase transitions in long-range quantum systems. Extending this analysis to other models, interaction exponents, or dynamical settings (e.g., quenches, Floquet protocols, or monitored dynamics) may yield new insights into the interplay between long-range interactions, classical criticality, and quantum complexity.

Appendix C Computing SRE for mixed states

To calculate the SRE we use Eq. 7 instead of Eq. 6 by enlarging the Pauli string operator and calculating T​r​[��​�​�~]2=⟨X�|​�​�~​|X�⟩2Tr[\rho_{\beta}\boldsymbol{\sigma\tilde{\sigma}}]^{2}=\bra{X_\beta}\boldsymbol{\sigma\tilde{\sigma}}\ket{X_\beta}^{2} with |X�⟩=∑s1�1⋯sN�NA1s1​�1⋯A1sN​�N|s1�1⋯sN�N⟩\ket{X_\beta}=\sum_{s_{1}\kappa_{1}\cdots s_{N}\kappa_{N}}\mdmathbb{A}_{1}^{s_{1}\kappa_{1}}\cdots\mdmathbb{A}_{1}^{s_{N}\kappa_{N}}\ket{s_1\kappa_1\cdots s_N\kappa_N} Fig. 12(a) while considering the Kraus indices of |X�⟩\ket{X_\beta} as the physical indices. As mentioned in the main text, we treat �i\kappa_{i} as another physical index, giving rise to an effective system size twice as large as the original one. The ideal way to deal with these extra legs is to calculate ⟨X�|​�​|X�⟩2\bra{X_\beta}\boldsymbol{\sigma}\ket{X_\beta}^{2} instead, by contracting the auxiliary leg with the corresponding conjugated one as shown in Fig.13(b). But the following are the issues for this choice:

  1. 1.

    To calculate ⟨X�|​�​�~​|X�⟩2\bra{X_\beta}\boldsymbol{\sigma\tilde{\sigma}}\ket{X_\beta}^{2} or ⟨X�|​�​|X�⟩2\bra{X_\beta}\boldsymbol{\sigma}\ket{X_\beta}^{2} we need 4 replicas of the MPS. In the first case, the calculation of the conditional probability is straightforward, and this is clear from the depiction of the �​(�1​�~1)\pi(\sigma_{1}\tilde{\sigma}_{1}) in Fig. 13(a). Whereas in Fig. 13(b) we can see the 44 replicas get inter-connected, which makes the analysis numerically costly. For example, if we start contracting from the gray shaded part in Fig. 13(b), the numerical cost is �6\mu^{6} (say, �\mu is the bond dimension), whereas for Fig. 13(a) it is �2\mu^{2}.

  2. 2.

    Arguably, the direct contraction of the auxiliary index is not a good approximation of calculating the SRE in the finite TT regime. When a mixed state is represented in terms of a possible MPS, there is an extra index at each site (Fig. 12(a)) that ensures an extra degree of freedom. For any practical purpose, this is considered just another physical leg. Therefore, in our T≠0T\neq 0 study, it will not be a good measure of magic if we only calculate ⟨X�|​�​|X�⟩2\bra{X_\beta}\boldsymbol{\sigma}\ket{X_\beta}^{2}.

Appendix D hch_{c} from DMRG

At T=0T=0, to get the idea of the critical field hch_{c}, we do a preliminary investigation of the quantum criticality by performing a DMRG calculation using the itensor library of Julia [21, 20]. The non-zero to zero transition of the magnetization, <sz><s^{z}>, indicates the quantum critical point here. In Fig. 14 we show how <sz><s^{z}> evolves as a function of hh, for N=200,280,300,340,360N=200,280,300,340,360 for each of �=\alpha= 1.81.8 and 0.80.8. We find hc≈1.55h_{c}\approx 1.55 for �=1.8\alpha=1.8 , whereas hc≈1.85h_{c}\approx 1.85 for �=0.8\alpha=0.8. In our discussion, the only nonzero hh value we consider is h=0.3h=0.3, and therefore, for both cases, this field value is far from the quantum critical point. This is the reason why the shift in �c\beta_{c} is very less as hh varies from 0.00.0 to 0.30.3 for both values of �\alpha ( see Table.1 ).
